name: CDICF transactional component installer
sovereign_question: Can this component land in this project, completely, reversibly, and lawfully — and can the operation be stopped mid-flight without leaving a tree nobody can explain?
scope: install a CPP Design Registry entry into a target project as a journalled transaction
verify installed artifacts against the checksums recorded at install time
roll back a committed install to its prior bytes
recover an interrupted or aborted transaction to the pre-transaction state
non_scope: choosing WHICH component to install — that is the selector, and this engine never selects
emitting registry entries — that is the emitter
retro-active uninstallation of installs committed in earlier sessions when the kill switch trips
any network fetch: every byte installed comes from the emitter output passed in
triggers: a component has been selected and approved for adoption into a project
an interrupted transaction is detected (a journal exists in <target>/.cdicf)
a drift check is requested against installed artifacts
an adopted component must be reverted
anti_triggers: the redistribution posture derived from the licence tier is 'prohibited' and the entry carries code — refused at exit 5
the kill switch is armed for the target project — refused at exit 12 before a journal is created
a declared dependency is unresolved in the target — refused at exit 11 before any write
prerequisites: emitter output (registry-item.json + install-manifest.json) for the component
required_evidence: per-artifact sha256 matching the install manifest
a recomputed roll-up checksum, never the manifest's own value taken on trust
postconditions read back from disk after the rename sweep
outputs: installed artifacts in the target tree
<target>/.cdicf/journal.json — present only while a transaction is open or aborted
<target>/.cdicf/aborted/<txid>.json — archived post-mortem of a kill-switch abort
consumers: the consuming project's build, which compiles the installed artifacts
modules/cdicf/selector.js — reads installed.json for the prior-adoption tiebreak
tools/design_index.py --components-sync — reads installed.json to mark index install state
modules/cdio scorer dependency-scope hard filter — reads installed.json to resolve registry dependencies
permissions: write inside the target project directory only
rollback: `node modules/cdicf/installer.js rollback --component <id> --target <proj>` reverts a committed install to its prior bytes, and is itself journalled so an interrupted rollback is recoverable. A file modified since install is reported as skipped rather than overwritten — recovery that over-reaches is a worse failure than recovery that stops and says so.
kill_switch: `node modules/cdicf/installer.js kill-switch arm --target <proj>` writes <target>/.cdicf/KILL_SWITCH. Armed, an install refuses at exit 12 BEFORE creating a journal; a transaction already running stops at its next phase seam — inside the rename sweep the in-flight renameSync completes (it is one atomic syscall) and the sweep stops before the next. The abort records ABORTED_BY_KILL_SWITCH with a timestamp, the phase, and the last durable journal state into installed.json, and PRESERVES the journal for post-mortem rather than deleting it. It does not roll back: the tree is returned to its pre-state by `installer.js recover`, which archives the journal to .cdicf/aborted/<txid>.json instead of discarding it. Installs committed in earlier sessions are untouched, by decision. A file rather than only a signal, because Node never emits SIGTERM on Windows and a signal-only switch would be inert on this estate's primary host; SIGTERM/SIGINT are additionally honoured where the platform delivers them, and the listeners are removed on every exit path. It does NOT auto-disarm — disarm with `kill-switch disarm --target <proj>`, named in every refusal, because a switch nobody can turn off is an outage.
retirement_condition: Retire when a project's package manager can install CPP registry components transactionally with equivalent provenance and recovery guarantees, making a CDICF-specific installer redundant.
